body:
**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Keep unverified adapters behind the raw-launch path**

Captain, this makes `cb` and `pioneer` first-class launch templates, so `config/crew-harness=cb`/`pioneer` or a per-task override will dispatch work through them without the raw-launch verification path. That conflicts with the adapter contract in `AGENTS.md` that says never dispatch an unverified adapter, and the new `cb` docs themselves still say it “Needs a smoke-test spawn”; `pioneer` has no matching documented adapter entry at all. Until these are empirically verified and documented, accepting them here can silently route real tasks to an adapter whose trust prompts, turn-end hook, or command availability have not been validated.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P1 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P1-orange?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Make the OpenCode backend helper executable**

This new helper is checked in with mode `100644`, but the backend invokes it directly as an executable from paths such as `fm-spawn` when `FM_BACKEND=opencode-server`. In that configuration the spawn path fails immediately with `Permission denied` before it can start the server; mark this file executable like the other `bin/` helpers.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P1 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P1-orange?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Make the OpenCode server test executable**

Captain, this test is also checked in with mode `100644`, while the new CI tests job runs each `test/*.test.sh` directly with `"$t"`. On the Ubuntu runner this file stops the job with `Permission denied`, so the backend contract tests cannot pass until the executable bit is set or the workflow invokes tests through `bash`.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Keep requiring the gh binary**

When bootstrap builds the required tool list, `gh` is no longer included. `gh-axi` is not a replacement for the underlying GitHub CLI; its own setup docs say “You still need gh installed and authenticated via gh auth login” (https://github.com/kunchenguid/gh-axi). On a fresh machine with `gh-axi` installed but no `gh`, this now reports only `NEEDS_GH_AUTH`, so the captain is told to run `gh auth login` but that command is missing and all GitHub-backed workflows remain blocked. Add `gh` back to the tool list and `install_cmd`.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Preserve the selected home for dashboard panes**

Captain, when this is invoked for a non-default firstmate home or with `FM_STATE_OVERRIDE`, the dashboard process created by tmux re-runs the script from tmux's session/global environment rather than this shell's resolved `FM_HOME`/override values; tmux only carries variables in `update-environment` or those passed with `-e VARIABLE=value`. In an existing tmux server those firstmate-specific variables are typically absent, so the command center falls back to the repo root and shows/links the wrong task state. Please pass the resolved home/override environment into the `new-session`/`new-window`/`respawn-pane` dashboard commands (and the split path).

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Drop the unsupported Droid --settings flag**

When `crew-harness` or a per-task override selects droid for a normal ship/scout task, this launch string passes `--settings`; I checked Factory's [CLI reference](https://docs.factory.ai/reference/cli-reference) and settings docs, which document flags such as `--auto`, `--cwd`, and `--append-system-prompt`, while settings are loaded from `~/.factory/settings.json` plus `.factory/settings.local.json`, not a `--settings` flag. On those droid spawns the CLI exits with an invalid option before reading the brief, so the new verified harness is unusable for regular crewmates; install the Stop hook through a supported `.factory` settings/hooks file or another documented mechanism instead.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P1 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P1-orange?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Use Cursor's direct command hook schema**

Captain, when spawning any cursor-backed task this writes the firstmate stop hook as a Claude-style nested entry (`{"hooks":[{"type":"command",...}]}`), but Cursor hook files define each `stop` item with a top-level `command` field (for example, the Cursor hooks article shows `"stop": [{"command": "but cursor stop"}]`: https://blog.gitbutler.com/cursor-hooks-deep-dive). Cursor will not run this nested object, so cursor crewmates never touch `state/<id>.turn-ended` and firstmate only notices completed turns via stale/heartbeat polling instead of the promised stop hook.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Require jq before spawning cursor tasks**

Captain, cursor spawns now rely on `jq` to install the shared `~/.cursor/hooks.json` stop hook, but bootstrap only reports missing `jq` for X mode or an active crew-dispatch file, not for a plain cursor harness setup. On a fresh machine without `jq`, this branch returns success after a warning, the task still launches and writes `.fm-cursor-turnend`, but Cursor never gets the hook that touches `state/<id>.turn-ended`, so firstmate falls back to stale polling for every cursor crewmate. Please make `jq` a detected prerequisite when cursor is selected, or fail cursor spawn before launching without the hook.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Fail closed when Cursor hook merge fails**

Captain, when an existing `~/.cursor/hooks.json` is malformed or has an unmergeable shape, this branch only warns and then the caller continues to write `.fm-cursor-turnend` and launch `cursor-agent`. In that scenario the shared stop hook was not installed, so Cursor has no command that can touch `state/<id>.turn-ended`; the task is reported as spawned even though the turn-end signal silently falls back to stale polling. Please return non-zero here (as the missing-`jq` path already does) so cursor spawns do not proceed without the required hook.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

Addressed in 024bb2b: switched to Cursor's documented flat schema `"stop": [{"command": "..."}]` (no nested `hooks` wrapper) and updated the test to match. The hook will now fire correctly for firstmate cursor sessions. (Latest related: ac8d2b0)

Addressed across ffcd980 + 2ff93cf + ac8d2b0:
- bootstrap now emits MISSING: jq when crew-harness or secondmate-harness is cursor.
- spawn fails hard (error + exit 1) before any window/agent if no jq for cursor.
- the merge function itself now errors on jq missing or on merge failure (no more soft warning+continue paths).

Addressed in ac8d2b0: the merge failure path (bad JSON, unmergeable, etc.) now does `error` + `exit 1` instead of warning and continuing the spawn. Cursor tasks will not launch without a working turn-end hook installed.

**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Detect cursor defaults before jq check**

Captain, this check only examines the literal `config/crew-harness` contents; if that file is absent or set to `default` while firstmate itself is running under `cursor-agent`, `fm-harness.sh crew` resolves to `cursor` but bootstrap will not emit `MISSING: jq`. This is a fresh gap beyond the earlier jq fix: cursor is selected implicitly via harness detection, so the first spawn fails in `fm-spawn.sh` instead of the session-start consent/install flow surfacing the prerequisite.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Parse secondmate harness before jq check**

Captain, this secondmate jq probe removes all whitespace before taking the first field, so documented `config/secondmate-harness` lines like `cursor auto high` are parsed as `cursorautohigh` and skip `MISSING: jq` on machines without jq. This is fresh evidence beyond the prior jq thread: the added parser disagrees with `fm-harness.sh`'s whitespace-token parser for pinned secondmate model/effort, so a cursor secondmate can pass bootstrap and then fail at spawn.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P1 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P1-orange?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Skip invalid recorded worktrees before safety checks**

In the normal non-Orca teardown path, this new guard is only reached after the dirty/unpushed checks have already run against `$WT`. When a pre-fix meta recorded the launch cwd or firstmate home and that directory is a git checkout with dirty or unpushed work, `fm-teardown.sh` exits with `REFUSED` before it reaches this graceful skip, so the window and meta remain stuck even though the recorded path is not safe to return. Apply the same `safe_task_worktree` decision before the landed-work checks, or otherwise bypass those checks for invalid recorded worktrees.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Increase the resurface test timeout**

Captain, this new test races the watcher’s own polling cadence: after flipping the fake herdr pane back to `idle`, the watcher may need one poll to record the new `agentstate:idle` signal and two more polls to reach the `n>=2` stale threshold, so the 40×0.1s budget is too tight once shell/herdr-stub overhead is included. I reproduced `bash tests/fm-watch-triage.test.sh` failing here with `not ok - watcher did not resurface a settled herdr pane after intervening work`; use a larger timeout or pre-seed the post-transition count so CI does not flake/fail on slower hosts.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

Addressed: enlarged wait_for_exit's budget in test_herdr_settled_stale_resurfaces_after_busy_transition from 40 to 200 ticks (4s to 20s). At FM_POLL=1s cadence, resurfacing after the idle flip needs one poll to record agentstate:idle plus two more to cross the n>=2 stale threshold, so 4s was too tight on slow hosts. Since the failure mode is hang-until-timeout, the larger budget costs nothing on the passing path. Fixed in 3399f9e.

**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Fetch the amend branch into a checkoutable ref**

For an amend PR whose head branch is not already present as a local/remote-tracking ref (for example a PR opened after the last fleet fetch, or a fork PR), this setup can block before any fix is attempted: Git documents `git fetch origin master` as shorthand for `master:`, meaning it fetches the branch without naming a remote-tracking ref to update, so the following `git checkout <branch>` has nothing to check out. Fetch into an explicit ref, check out `FETCH_HEAD`, or use a PR-checkout flow that handles forks before asking the crewmate to verify and push the existing PR branch.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Filter orphan statuses from the afk daemon scan**

Captain, this guard only runs inside the child watcher’s signal scan. In away mode the supervising daemon still has its own housekeeping catch-all (`bin/fm-supervise-daemon.sh`'s `scan_captain_relevant_statuses` loop) that scans every `state/*.status` without requiring matching `.meta`; an orphan `ghost.status` containing `done:` is still added to `.subsuper-escalations` as a catch-all scan if housekeeping sees it, so the promised “never surfaced, even under afk” behavior is not upheld. Please apply the same meta filter to the daemon catch-all path (or the shared scanner) before relying on this guarantee.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Recheck meta after signal coalescing**

Captain, this guard only filters files at the moment `scan_signals` runs, but entries captured before `SIGNAL_GRACE` are still classified after the sleep even if teardown removes `state/<id>.meta` during that grace window. In that teardown race, the old pending row reaches `signal_crew_provably_working`, `fm-crew-state` sees no meta and returns `none`, and the watcher enqueues a signal wake for an unowned file despite the new orphan guarantee. Revalidate the coalesced pending set against matching `.meta` files before classification/queueing.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Propagate no-mistakes installer failures**

When `bin/fm-bootstrap.sh install no-mistakes` uses this new helper and the helper fails closed (for example a checksum mismatch, missing asset, or download failure), the surrounding install loop still exits 0 because it `eval`s the returned command without checking its status. That makes the documented bootstrap install path report success even though no verified `no-mistakes` binary was installed, so callers can proceed with the required gate tool still missing.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P1 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P1-orange?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Skip lifecycle imports in read-only sessions**

When this is a read-only captain session because another firstmate holds the lock, this still runs `fm-lifecycle-import.sh`, which calls `fm-lifecycle.sh register` for legacy `state/*.meta` records and writes `*.lifecycle`/`*.events` files. That violates the lock/refusal contract and can race with the session that actually owns state; the read-only branch should skip mutating import work or run only a dry-run equivalent.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P1 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P1-orange?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Avoid reaping live tasks during session startup**

On a locked session start this applies the heartbeat reaper before the digest's endpoint/status reconciliation can prove whether a recorded crewmate is still alive; any active lifecycle record older than the default TTL+grace is closed as `interrupted` solely from `heartbeat_at`. If firstmate was stopped, the watcher paused, or a live task simply had no recent positive working evidence for ~20 minutes, restart marks it interrupted even though its backend endpoint may still be alive, and later watcher logic ignores non-`active` lifecycle records.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Clean up Git worktrees when backend spawn fails**

For non-Orca spawns this creates and registers the Git worktree before the tmux/herdr/zellij/cmux task window is created and before any meta/lifecycle record or cleanup trap exists. If the later backend creation fails, for example an existing `fm-<id>` window or a backend CLI error, the script exits and leaves an untracked linked worktree behind with no state record for teardown or the lifecycle reaper to find.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P1 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P1-orange?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Kill the crew before force-removing worktrees**

Captain, checked `git worktree remove -h`: `-f` forces removal even if the worktree is dirty or locked. In this non-Orca teardown path, the recorded backend is killed only after this call, so if the pane is still alive and writes after `validate_worktree_teardown_safety` but before removal, this forced remove can discard uncommitted work that the safety check never saw, violating the teardown contract. Stop the backend before the final safety/remove step or avoid forced removal here.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P1 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P1-orange?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Handle status updates after blocked states**

Once a task appends `blocked:` or `needs-decision:`, this code moves its lifecycle out of `active`; later status lines are skipped by this guard. In the common captain-decision flow where the crew then appends `resolved:`/`working:`/`done:`, the lifecycle stays `blocked`/`needs-decision`, and `fm-teardown.sh` later aborts because the transition policy does not allow those states to close out as `completed`. This leaves finished tasks impossible to clean up and still counted by admission/WIP.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Avoid hard-coded cockpit paths**

This new tracked executable is tied to one user's checkout and log path. On any other Firstmate home, or the same home under `FM_HOME`/`FM_ROOT` overrides, it will `cd` into non-existent `/Users/ryanfong/...` directories and write logs outside the active home, so the scheduled refresh cannot run for other installations. Resolve these paths from environment/default home settings or require explicit overrides instead of fixed absolute paths.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P1 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P1-orange?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Launch session backends from the linked worktree**

Captain, after creating the disposable Git worktree here, the non-Orca backend windows/tabs are still created with `$PROJ_ABS`, and the old `treehouse get` step that moved the pane into the worktree was removed. For normal ship/scout spawns the harness therefore starts in the primary checkout while hooks and metadata point at `$WT`, so a crewmate can branch or commit in the primary checkout even though `validate_spawn_worktree` passes.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P1 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P1-orange?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Let restore spawns skip their own admission record**

When recovery or liveness respawns an existing task ID, notably `fm-bootstrap.sh` calling `fm-spawn.sh "$id" --secondmate`, the task can already have an active `$STATE/$ID.lifecycle` with the same objective. This admission call runs before `register_task`'s `FM_LIFECYCLE_RESTORE` path, so `fm-lifecycle-admit.sh` sees the task's own record as a duplicate and exits, preventing dead secondmates from being respawned once lifecycle state exists.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Close lifecycle only after teardown succeeds**

If any later cleanup step fails after this closeout, such as `git worktree remove` refusing a locked registered worktree or backend/home cleanup erroring, teardown exits with runtime/meta still present but the lifecycle already marked terminal `completed` or `abandoned`. That drops the task from WIP and reaper tracking and makes a retry look finished before cleanup actually happened, so the lifecycle receipt should be written only after the destructive cleanup succeeds or be rolled back on failure.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P1 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P1-orange?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Keep Claude crews able to report status**

Captain, when Claude is the resolved/default harness, this bounded launch starts in `acceptEdits` without granting access to Firstmate's state/data paths; the generated briefs require every ship/scout to append `echo ... >> $STATE/$ID.status` and scouts to write `$DATA/$ID/report.md`, both outside the task worktree. [Anthropic's permission-mode docs](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/permission-modes) state that `acceptEdits` auto-approval is scoped to the working directory or configured additional directories, so these required outside-path writes will prompt and leave unattended Claude crews unable to report progress or finish unless the bounded profile explicitly includes those paths.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P1 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P1-orange?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Do not apply passthrough fields to record internals**

When an event carries an extra field such as `fields.status`, this assignment copies it straight onto the folded record because `recordFieldsSchema` is `passthrough()`. A valid `retired` event with `fields.status: 'active'` would pass schema validation, run the transition, and then leave the terminal record active, bypassing the state machine and active-index filtering; restrict application to the known mutable record fields or strip unknown keys before folding.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Fail doctor when the active index is not current**

When the registry is healthy but `memory-index.json` is missing or stale, `auditRegistry()` reports `activeIndex.status !== 'current'`, but this health gate ignores `parts.activeIndex` entirely. That lets `mem doctor` exit 0 even though consumers would read an out-of-date or absent active-memory index, so the doctor result should include the active-index status in its `ok` calculation.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Canonicalize case aliases, not only symlinks**

Captain, in the macOS case-insensitive path-alias scenario this helper still uses `cd "$path" && pwd -P`, which resolves symlinks/physical `..` components but does not re-enumerate path components to a single on-disk casing; the added tests only cover a symlink alias. If the lock records `/Users/...` and the current harness reaches the same directory as `/users/...`, both calls can still return differently-cased strings, so `fm_watcher_lock_matches_pid` continues to reject the healthy watcher and `--restart` can still no-op for the original bug this change is meant to fix.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P1 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P1-orange?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Restore fm-lock parsing before session startup**

Captain, this added nested `if` leaves the outer `if` from the previous line without a matching `fi`, so `bash -n bin/fm-lock.sh` fails with a syntax error at the loop's `done`. Any path that invokes `fm-lock.sh` (including session start and `status`) will abort before acquiring or inspecting the fleet lock.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P1 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P1-orange?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Require the newly acquired worktree, not merely the same repo**

Captain, when the transient cwd is another existing linked worktree of the requested repository, this predicate accepts it because its Git common directory matches. The spawn loop then records that other task's worktree, installs hooks there, and launches a second agent into it, risking cross-task edits; correlate the candidate with the worktree acquired by this `treehouse get` invocation rather than accepting any non-primary worktree from the repository.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P1 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P1-orange?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Preserve project-setting isolation for legacy gate runs**

Captain, when an older or external no-mistakes validation runs (a scenario explicitly retained in `docs/architecture.md`), deleting this trusted `disable_project_settings: true` setting makes the gate agent load the root `AGENTS.md` and assume the fleet-captain identity. The remaining refusal is only sourced by `fm-spawn.sh`, `fm-send.sh`, `fm-teardown.sh`, and the session-start nudge; the mandated `fm-session-start.sh` itself can still acquire the live `FM_HOME` lock, drain wakes, sync projects, and restart secondmates. Keep a minimal tracked configuration that disables project settings even though normal self-delivery no longer uses no-mistakes.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Check the committed range for whitespace errors**

Because step 4 commits the changes before this command runs, a clean contributor worktree makes bare `git diff --check` inspect only the empty working-tree-versus-index diff and succeed without checking the submitted commit. This matches the no-commit form shown by `git diff -h`; use an explicit range such as `origin/main...HEAD` so the required verification actually covers the branch.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Push fork contributors to their fork remote**

For an external contributor following step 1, `origin` is explicitly reset to the parent repository, so this command attempts to push to `kunchenguid/firstmate` and fails without maintainer write access; the fork is never configured as another remote. Add a contributor-owned remote and push there, or have contributors clone their fork and retain the parent as an `upstream` remote.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Update the Pi live regression for the advisory contract**

With `FM_PI_LIVE_E2E=1`, `tests/fm-pi-primary-live-e2e.test.sh:125-135` deliberately creates an unhealthy watcher and then waits for the `TURN WOULD END BLIND` follow-up before it can arm the watcher. The new exit-0 guard means Pi no longer sends that follow-up, so this supported live regression deterministically times out; revise or replace that scenario to exercise the new advisory/recovery path.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P1 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P1-orange?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Surface advisories for passive harness adapters**

When work is in flight and supervision is missing, this exit-0 result causes the OpenCode and Pi adapters to return at their `result.code !== 2` branches (`.opencode/plugins/fm-primary-turnend-guard.js:73-74`, `.pi/extensions/fm-primary-turnend-guard.ts:138-139`), while the Grok adapter discards the captured stderr and exits (`bin/fm-turnend-guard-grok.sh:32-34`). Thus all three supported passive harnesses silently end the turn without receiving the recovery instruction, turning the former recovery path into no notification at all; deliver the advisory through each harness's user-visible mechanism without forcing a follow-up.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P1 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P1-orange?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Reject brace and glob expansion in teardown arguments**

Captain, when a teardown argument uses brace or glob expansion, the lexer sets `unquotedExpansion` but leaves `literal` true, so this check allows commands such as `bin/fm-teardown.sh {task,--force}`. Bash expands that command to the arguments `task` and `--force`, and `fm-teardown.sh:106` treats the second argument as force mode, bypassing the dirty, unlanded-work, and scout-report safeguards that this recovery gate is intended to protect; include `argument.unquotedExpansion` in the unsafe classification.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P1 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P1-orange?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Sanitize the prompt before using the restricted lane**

When the captain uses the normal scout/ship intake with this DeepSeek model, this launch still sends `$(cat __BRIEF__)` verbatim to the external model. The standard generated scout brief includes local project context plus absolute report/status paths and lifecycle instructions (for example `bin/fm-brief.sh` lines 234, 244, 262, and 264), so disabling context files and tools does not actually prevent private local metadata from reaching the model. This lane needs to build/pass a sanitized public-only prompt, or refuse standard briefs, before the restricted launch is used.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Align complete_scout's normal-completion order**

For a normal restricted scout, these model-facing guidelines say `complete_scout` should be called after `write_report`, but the false branch later tells the model to call `write_report` after `complete_scout`, and only `append_status(done)` actually marks the task complete. In practice a model following the guidelines can write the report, call `complete_scout(false)`, then be instructed to rewrite/continue instead of finishing, leaving the scout parked or producing duplicate final writes; make `complete_scout` either the final terminating tool or the pre-report decision check, but not both.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Restrict the DeepSeek lane to scout tasks**

Because this predicate accepts every non-secondmate kind, a normal ship spawn using `--harness pi --model deepseek/deepseek-v4-pro` is routed into the report-only restricted launch. **Detached descendants escape cleanup** When an adapter starts a long-lived descendant in a new session or process group, `groupAlive`, `signalGroup`, and `cleanupGroup` continue tracking only the entrypoint's process group. The invocation can therefore finish or time out while the detached descendant keeps running indefinitely, leaking processes and resources across repeated polls.

**Reparented descendants escape cleanup** When an adapter spawns a detached long-lived process and exits before the next process-table refresh, the child reparents to PID 1 before this PPID-only traversal records it. The process then falls outside signaling and leak detection, so it survives normal completion or timeout and accumulates resources across polls.

**Tracker failure leaks adapter** When the marker-enabled process-table query fails after the pre-spawn check succeeds, `startProcessTracker` throws after the adapter has already been spawned, leaving that process unsignaled and able to continue indefinitely.

**Changed CWD escapes cleanup** When a detached, marker-free descendant changes its working directory before the tracker observes it, `packageChild` remains false after reparenting and the process is never added to `tracker.descendants`. Because it is also outside the entrypoint process group, completion and timeout cleanup leave it running indefinitely.

**Reparented descendants escape cleanup** When an adapter rapidly starts a detached long-lived descendant that sanitizes its environment, changes its working directory, and executes a different binary before the tracker refreshes, neither the marker, package-root, nor root-executable check adopts it. The descendant remains outside `tracker.descendants`, causing invocation completion or timeout cleanup to leave it running indefinitely.

The reported case is now: a worker whose counters have been *observed moving*, then spends 25+ minutes in one call with no token, spend, or context movement, no status append, no completed turn, no busy-state transition, and no write anywhere in its own task worktree. A counter-free harness no longer reaches this branch at all.

Against that, the alternative is what this change exists to fix: two workers frozen for twenty minutes and an hour with no notification whatsoever, one holding six commits of unpublished work, found only because a human went looking.

The report is sized for that trade-off rather than pretending it away. The fuse defaults to 1500s — above the longest legitimate single call observed on this machine (22 minutes) and far above the 240s ordinary wedge threshold. The wording is `busy but no progress for Ns`, never wedged, blocked, stopped, or dead, so a supervisor reads it as "look at this", not "this is broken". It takes no action of any kind. **Unrelated processes block invocation** When an unrelated long-lived same-user process starts and reparents to PID 1 during an extension invocation, `ambiguousInvocationOrphans` attributes it from timing and reparenting alone and persists it in the extension quarantine. The current invocation fails with `process-attribution-ambiguous`, and later invocations remain blocked with `process-quarantined` until the unrelated process exits.

**Zero cannot prove blockage** When admission to a named stage varies between draws, this rule treats one class producing zero findings while peers clear the stage as proof that no later draw can change the result, causing workers to stop and report an unsupported structural conclusion as complete.

**Scout assertion misses clauses** The scout output is checked only for the rule's opening sentence, so the test still passes when its single-draw carve-out or complete-outcome framing is removed from the generated scout brief.

**Stale marker survives reassignment** When a pooled worktree is reassigned and writing its new ownership marker fails, spawn continues while the previous task's marker remains. A stale record for the previous task can then validate the reassigned worktree and terminate the new task's live processes. **How this was verified:** The worktree-return path does not remove `fm-task-owner`, the next spawn continues after an overwrite failure, and validation accepts the retained task and token.

**The identity check.** `bin/fm-worktree-proc-lib.sh:784` — the last thing `fm_wtproc_disposable_worktree` does before printing the accepted path:

```sh
  fm_wtproc_owns_root "$real" worktree "$id" "$token" || return 1
```

and the same line for the temp root at `:852`. `fm_wtproc_owns_root` (`:726`) accepts only when the root carries an allocation marker naming **this task and this allocation token**, and distinguishes its three refusals — no marker, another task, another allocation of this task — because they mean different things to whoever reads the report.

The marker is written by `bin/fm-spawn.sh` at allocation and its token recorded in `state/<id>.meta`; the readers take both id and token from that record, so path shape no longer participates in the decision. A worktree's marker lives in its per-worktree git directory, so it never appears in `git status`, never blocks teardown's dirty check, and never reaches a commit.

**An unmarked root is refused, not accepted.** A copy allocated before this binding and a reused path are indistinguishable, so the reading that stops is the one taken. That costs automatic cleanup on pre-existing copies, and is stated as such where the refusal surfaces.

**Pinned by** `test_a_root_that_matches_the_path_but_not_the_allocation_is_refused` in `tests/fm-worktree-proc.test.sh`, which covers all four cases on the exact recorded path — no marker, a different allocation of the same task, another task entirely, and a control arm proving a correctly stamped root is still accepted (without it the three refusals could come from a validator that refuses everything). It closes with the end-to-end shape your finding describes: a linked worktree reassigned to another task, a live process inside it, a cleanup driven from the stale record that still names it — and asserts that process is still running afterwards.

**The other half, which your summary comment named separately and which was the real remaining hole.** A reassigned copy still holds the previous holder's marker, and overwriting it is the only thing that retires it — so a marker write that failed left this task working in a copy carrying somebody else's identity, while spawn merely warned and carried on. Every failure on that path now refuses the spawn (unmintable token, unresolvable root, unwritable marker), each naming which. Fixed in `4782d96`, and the finding was right: the destructive path was accepting shape where the other two required ownership.

**The check.** `validate_recorded_reap_roots` now ends each root with `fm_wtproc_owns_root "$real" "$marker_kind" "$ID" "$OWNER_TOKEN"`, taking the task id and the allocation token from the record, and a root that cannot produce a matching marker refuses the teardown rather than narrowing it — signalling nothing and then running the destructive half against a record the safe half rejected is the worse outcome. `OWNER_TOKEN` is read alongside `WT` and `TASK_TMP`; the two roots keep their markers in different places, so the check is told which kind it is looking at.

**`--force` does not reach past it.** The check sits outside every `FORCE` branch, deliberately: forcing past an ownership refusal is precisely what stopped a live agent on 2026-08-27, so insisting is the one thing that must not work here. Pinned by its own arm in the test.

**The clone shape is included, not exempted.** This was the open design question, and it was decided the way that keeps the guarantee uniform: a spawn stamps every copy it allocates whatever its shape, and a clone keeps its marker in its own `.git` directory just as a linked worktree keeps it in its per-worktree git directory. So teardown still supports the ordinary-clone copy its suite pins — that case now stamps its fixture and passes — and that shape gains the same proof as the others. The check is still not `fm_wtproc_disposable_worktree`, whose linked-worktree proof would refuse the clone; ownership and shape stay separate questions.

**Refusals are actionable.** A copy allocated before this binding carries no marker and will be refused, so that message is the one an operator meets while cleaning up older work. Each refusal now names the marker file it looked for, which of the four causes it was (no recorded token, no marker, another task, another allocation of this task), and what to do — correct the record when the copy is someone else's, or write the two marker lines deliberately when it really is this task's. The remedy is the marker rather than a flag on purpose: adopting a copy should be something someone did after looking at what is running in it.

**Pinned by** `test_a_copy_that_cannot_be_shown_to_be_this_tasks_refuses_teardown` in `tests/fm-teardown.test.sh`. Both arms run against an otherwise perfectly ordinary copy, so the teardown genuinely reaches the signalling loop and the refusal is this check rather than something upstream. Arm one strips the marker; arm two stamps it for another task — the reassignment case itself — and both assert a live process in that copy is still running afterwards, that the copy and the record survive, and that the refusal names its cause and the marker path. **The principle is real.** `VISION.md` line 23 does say new capability "ships as an option to enable, never as behavior that assumes consent." In the general case that would land.

**But `VISION.md` line 30 resolves this exact conflict:** "A current, explicit captain instruction outranks any standing rule the first mate wrote for itself, exactly as stated and no further."

The captain issued precisely such an instruction for this change. The accepted acceptance criteria are that plain `bin/fm-test-run.sh --changed` is **repeatably under five minutes**, and an explicit hard constraint forbids **hiding the suite from the normal developer path**. Requiring `--jobs` to get the fast path violates both: it leaves the default path serial (~818s for the watcher family alone) and gates the fix behind a flag.

That matters concretely rather than theoretically. This PR exists because an agent ran plain `--changed`, it took ~29m29s, and it was killed mid-run against a 30-minute budget and invisibly retried all day. A flag-gated fast path leaves that agent — and every developer who types the obvious command — on exactly the path that caused the incident.

**On the substance of "assumes consent":** this isn't new capability shipping on by default. It's a scheduling characteristic of an existing command whose contract is unchanged: the same scripts run, the same assertions, the same results. Only wall-clock changes, from ~818s to ~210s. Consent is also still fully available in both directions — an explicit `--jobs` always wins, including `--jobs 1` to force serial — and every other selection mode and CI lane keeps its existing default, byte-identical in behavior.

The concurrency itself is not assumed either: it is admitted only for scripts with a recorded concurrency proof (`bin/fm-test-isolation-proof.sh --pool <family>`, evidence in `docs/fm-test-isolation-proof.md`), it is bounded at min(4, cpus), and any unproven script still runs serially after the concurrent group rather than beside it.

This finding was filed against 8809efcb, before the lock landed.

On the current head it is not reachable:

1. `cmd_reap` acquires `$STATE/.control-<id>.lock` before `scan_task` and holds it through `fm_wtproc_reap` (released on EXIT). Contention refuses rather than waits, so a scan that authorised an ownerless stop cannot be acted on after a relaunch has taken the same lock.
2. `bin/fm-control.sh` acquires that same lock at the top of every verb, including relaunch, before it stops the old agent, launches the replacement (`fm-spawn --relaunch`), and waits for it to come up. The replacement cannot occupy the reused roots while a reap holds the lock, and a reap cannot signal while relaunch holds it.
3. `bin/fm-lease-lib.sh` is a different contract (`$STATE/.lease-<task>`): which Pi supervision actor (main vs branch) may mutate a task. It is not the process-signalling lock. Relaunch takes the lease, then the control lock. The race described here is serialised by the control lock alone.

Regression: `tests/fm-worktree-proc.test.sh` `test_a_lifecycle_action_in_flight_blocks_the_stop` — a live process holds this task's control lock with every other reap gate open; the reap refuses and the witness survives; once the lock is released, the same reap stops it.
